title: An-Nas: the people
hookLine: refuge with the Lord of people from the whisperer who withdraws (Surah 114)

lines: THE LAST SURAH OF THE QUR'AN.
cards: It's two in the morning. The house is quiet, and a voice in your head is not. You're not good enough.
They were laughing at you. Check your phone one more time. It doesn't shout.
It whispers, and it's very patient. The Qur'an's last surah, number one hundred fourteen, is about exactly this voice: six short lines, and a picture of the whisperer that surprises people.
It sneaks in, and it slips away. Today the reading starts on the Qur'an's final page and works backward. Today: An-Nas, the people.

teach.b: Pickthall translates the opening: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind, The King of mankind, The God of mankind. Mankind, three times.
In Arabic it's an-nas, the people, and every line of the surah ends on that sound: nas, nas, nas, then khannas, then nas twice more. Read aloud, it rocks like a lullaby.

Allah is named three ways: Lord, the one who raises and cares for you; King, the one in charge; God, the one who is worshipped. Three doors to the same refuge. The danger is named once, in two words: al-waswas al-khannas.
Waswas is the whisper, a word that sounds like what it means.

teach.h: KHANNAS — THE ONE WHO DRAWS BACK.
teach.b: Khannas means the one who draws back, who shrinks away and hides. Commentators explain the picture: the whisperer comes when you forget Allah, and retreats when you remember Him.
In that picture, the whisper can't hold its ground against remembrance; it works best unnoticed. The surah ends by saying the whisperers come from among the jinn and from among people.
Some of the voices that pull you down are unseen. Some have phone numbers.

Aisha reports in Bukhari that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had a habit with these last surahs: every night before sleep he would cup his hands, recite al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas into them, and wipe his hands over his body, three times.
So for Muslims who keep that habit, the last page of the book is also the last thing said before the lights go out.

how: Many Muslims recite Surah an-Nas with al-Falaq and al-Ikhlas before sleep, blowing lightly into cupped hands and wiping them over the body, following the Prophet's practice; it is also recited after the prayers and for protection.

o: the people: the last surah, seeking refuge from whispers
the travelers: a prayer said before setting out on a journey
the prophets: a surah retelling earlier messengers

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.

s: An-Nas is the last surah of the Qur'an
the surah says whisperers are only unseen beings
it says they come from the jinn and from people.
the whisperer in the surah is loud and forceful
khannas: it sneaks in and draws back when Allah is remembered.

games.q: it's night, and the Prophet is going to sleep. what does Aisha say he did first?
o: recited the last three surahs into cupped hands and wiped his body
sat silent until he fell asleep
games.why: he recited al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas into his hands and wiped them over his body, three times (Bukhari). the book's last page became his last words of the day.

practice: Let one recent whisper come to mind, the kind that sounds like your own voice but isn't kind, and don't argue with it; just name it: that's a whisper.
If you pray, you can say the surah's first line, qul a'udhu bi rabbin-nas, and let it be the remembering. Then watch what the whisper does when it's looked at directly.

wordCard.voice: An-Nas. The people, the name of the Qur'an's last surah: refuge in the Lord of people from the whisperer who draws back. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the people, mankind. every line of Surah 114 ends on this sound.

carryVoice: Your line: the whisperer withdraws. Lord, King, God: three doors to one refuge. One hundred fifty-nine, in the books.
